notes.title: Chapter map: Production services
notes.html:
A Python service in production is an event loop calling unreliable things on behalf of impatient clients. Every note is either the serving shape (73, 77, 78), surviving failure (74, 75, 76, 80) or seeing what happened (79 sits between: it saves calls; 81, 82 record them). Read each arrow as a sentence: idempotency built on reliability mechanics.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 73 ASGI & workers ─▶ 74 reliability ─▶ 75 idempotency ─▶ 76 rate limiting ─▶ 77 streaming ─▶ 78 connection pools ─▶ 79 caching ─▶ 80 queues & workers ─▶ 81 structured logging ─▶ 82 observability

🌳 A call failed: retry it?

The reliability tools in 74–76 are alternatives for one decision, so it lives here (moved from note 74).

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • ❌ fail now (reliability): if the "4xx" is really a gateway's 408 or 409 conflict on a lock, it may be transient; classify by meaning, not range.
  • 🔑 key or don't retry (idempotency): if the operation is naturally idempotent (full-state PUT, upsert), retry freely without a key.
  • 🚦 honour Retry-After (rate limiting): if 429s are routine, your client-side bucket is sized above the quota; fix the budget, not the retry.
  • 🛡️ fail fast or over (breakers): if every provider's breaker is open, serve a cached or degraded answer (caching).
  • 🔁 backoff + jitter: if the work can wait minutes, hand it to a queue instead of holding a request open.
  • ⏱️ surface it: if retries keep starting past the budget, the ladder is too long for the SLO; shorten it.

🌳 Which streaming transport?

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • 🔌 WebSocket (streaming): if the only client message is "stop", use SSE plus a plain POST /cancel and skip the upgrade and stickiness.

  • 📡 SSE (streaming): if a proxy in the path buffers responses and can't be configured, fall back to long polling for that client.

  • ⏳ long polling: if events become continuous, the reconnect per event costs more than SSE's one open line.

  • 🔄 short polling: if freshness matters more than a few seconds, it's the wrong tool at any interval.

  • The one big idea: every mechanism here exists because something is unknown: whether a call succeeded (75), whether the upstream recovers (74), whether the client is still there (77), which request a log line belongs to (81). The fixes make the unknown explicit: keys, breakers, cancellation, context.

  • The two most-confused pairs: concurrency vs parallelism in a worker (73: coroutines vs processes) · rate limiting vs backpressure (76: admission at the edge vs flow through the pipeline).

  • Ten minutes before an interview: 74's breaker state diagram, 75's timeout-then-replay sequence, 77's pull-loop sequence, then the retry tree above.

  • Cross-chapter: the event loop (what every note here runs on) · context managers (lifespan, pools, transactions) · cancellation (timeouts and disconnects are both cancellation).

notes.title: ASGI vs WSGI & the Worker Model
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 ASGI specification · 📜 PEP 3333: WSGI · 📘 FastAPI: concurrency and async / await · 📘 FastAPI: server workers · 📘 FastAPI: lifespan events

⚡ TL;DR

WSGI is a sync call that holds a thread per request; ASGI is async app(scope, receive, send), where a response is a sequence of send messages. One worker = one process, one GIL, one event loop: coroutines give concurrency inside it, workers give parallelism across cores.

🧭 Flow: uvicorn parses HTTP into a scope ─▶ middleware chain, last-added outermost ─▶ router matches ─▶ dependencies + Pydantic validate (or 422) ─▶ async def awaited on the loop, def sent to a 40-thread pool ─▶ response sent back out as messages

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
ASGI vs WSGI in one line? WSGI: sync app(environ, start_response), a thread per request, no streaming. ASGI: async app(scope, receive, send), thousands in flight per worker.
async def vs def endpoint? async def runs on the event loop; def goes to anyio's threadpool, 40 threads by default.
How many uvicorn workers? About one per core: each is a process with its own GIL and loop.
What runs once per worker vs per request? lifespan (pools, clients) per worker; dependency resolution per request.
What breaks an SSE stream in middleware? Anything that reads response.body_iterator to log or rewrite it: the whole stream is buffered.
✏️ Draw by hand: one worker scope ─▶ middleware (outside-in) ─▶ router ─▶ DI + validation ─▶ fork: loop or threadpool ─▶ send messages back out.

💡 The idea

WSGI blocks a thread until the response is ready, so concurrency is capped at thread count, and an LLM call idles that thread for 5–30 s. ASGI makes the response a sequence of send calls, so one worker holds thousands of waiting requests at coroutine cost, and streaming is native. Measured with FastAPI 0.142.2 / Starlette 1.7.0 on CPython 3.12, driving the app's ASGI callable directly:

GET /sse  (async generator yields every 0.3 s)
0.02 s  http.response.start
0.02 s  http.response.body  b'data: 0\n\n'
0.32 s  http.response.body  b'data: 1\n\n'
0.62 s  http.response.body  b'data: 2\n\n'

Each yield is its own message, so time to first token is 20 ms, not the whole answer. A def endpoint reported its thread as AnyIO worker thread, an async def one as MainThread: the dispatch fork is real, and it decides who can block whom.

The trade: ASGI multiplexes thousands of waits on one loop and streams natively, and in exchange one blocking call inside async def stalls every request on that worker.

⚙️ How it works

One request inside one worker (markers match the Code section):

Rule What actually happens
Middleware order add_middleware wraps the app, so the last added is outermost: adding A then B ran B, then A, on the request.
Dependencies Resolved per request from the signature's Depends() graph, cached within that request: pull-based, closer to React hooks than Spring beans.
The fork async def must be async all the way down; def buys blocking safety at threadpool scale (40) instead of loop scale (thousands).
Workers uvicorn --workers N (or fastapi run --workers N) forks N full interpreters; uvicorn now manages and restarts them, replacing the gunicorn-with-uvicorn-workers pattern.
lifespan is per worker It's an async context manager bracketing a worker's life, so every pool inside it multiplies by N.

💻 Code

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
import httpx

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):            # ① once PER WORKER: 4 workers = 4 pools
    app.state.http = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(30.0, connect=5.0))
    yield                                    #   the worker serves requests here
    await app.state.http.aclose()            #   graceful shutdown drains the pool

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=8000)   # ② junk rejected before paying tokens

def http_client(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    return request.app.state.http            # DI hands out the SHARED client

@app.post("/v1/chat/stream")
async def stream_chat(req: ChatRequest,      # ③ async def: runs on the loop
                      client: httpx.AsyncClient = Depends(http_client)):
    async def tokens():
        async for chunk in call_llm(client, req.prompt):
            yield f"data: {chunk}\n\n"       # ④ each yield = one ASGI body message
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(tokens(), media_type="text/event-stream")

The handler returns at once with an unexecuted generator; Starlette drives it after http.response.start, interleaved with every other request on the loop.

⚠️ Break it: a "log the response" middleware on a streaming route.

@app.middleware("http")
async def log_body(request, call_next):
    resp = await call_next(request)
    body = b"".join([c async for c in resp.body_iterator])   # read it all to log it
    log.info("response %d bytes", len(body))
    return Response(body, status_code=resp.status_code, headers=dict(resp.headers))
# look for: when the first byte reaches the client
# naive model predicts: chunks still stream; middleware only observes

Same SSE route, same Starlette 1.7.0: http.response.start and all three chunks arrived together at 0.91 s. The client saw nothing for the whole generation; with a long LLM answer that's a proxy timeout. @app.middleware("http") alone streams fine on current Starlette; reading the body is what buffers. For cross-cutting work on a streaming service, write pure ASGI middleware that wraps send and passes body messages through untouched (streaming transport).

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: WSGI is a synchronous contract: the server calls app(environ, start_response) and blocks a thread until the response is ready, so concurrency caps at thread count. ASGI is async and message-based, app(scope, receive, send), so a response is a sequence of sends, which makes streaming and WebSockets first-class and lets one worker hold thousands of idle requests. A worker is one process, one GIL and one loop: run about one per core.

Q · Mechanism — Walk a request from uvicorn to your handler. Where do DI, validation and the threadpool fork happen? uvicorn parses HTTP in C, builds the scope and calls the outermost middleware; the chain forwards to Starlette's router. FastAPI then resolves the handler's dependency graph and validates the body with Pydantic; a failure is a 422 before your code runs. Then the fork: a coroutine function is awaited on the loop; a plain def, and sync dependencies, go to anyio's 40-thread pool so they can block safely. The real trap is the inverse: blocking calls inside async def.

Q · Failure — After a teammate added logging middleware, the SSE chat endpoint shows nothing until it times out. Diagnose. The middleware consumes response.body_iterator to log or rewrite the body, so it waits for the generator to finish before sending anything; headers and chunks then arrive together (0.91 s in Break it, minutes for a long answer). Fix: log metadata only, or write pure ASGI middleware with async __call__(scope, receive, send) that wraps send, adjusts http.response.start and passes body chunks through: O(1) memory, streaming-safe. Then add a test asserting first-chunk latency through the full middleware stack.

Q · Design — An LLM gateway must serve 10K concurrent SSE streams per region on 4-core pods. Topology, shared state, and what breaks first? Four workers per pod, each holding ~2.5K coroutine-cheap streams. Everything in lifespan is per worker: 4 × an httpx pool of 500 is 2,000 upstream connections, 4 × an asyncpg pool of 20 is 80 DB connections per pod (pool math). Workers share nothing, so rate limits and caches move to Redis. What breaks first: a blocking call collapsing one worker's streams, then httpx's default 100-connection pool silently serializing fan-out, then fd limits. I'd watch loop lag p99 first.

⚖️ Compare

FastAPI Flask Django + DRF Starlette
Protocol ASGI WSGI WSGI or ASGI ASGI
Validation Pydantic built in external DRF serializers bring your own
Streaming, WebSockets native no limited native
Best for IO-bound APIs, LLM and SSE serving small sync services CRUD with ORM, admin, auth bare ASGI

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "FastAPI is faster than Flask"
    ✅ Per request it's comparable; it's cheaper per concurrent connection for IO-bound work.
  • ❌ "Declaring async def makes the endpoint concurrent"
    ✅ Only if everything inside is awaited on non-blocking clients.
    ↳ Worse: async def around a sync SDK serializes every request; plain def would at least get the threadpool (bridging).
  • 🔀 Not the same: workers vs coroutines
    ↳ Difference: coroutines give concurrency inside one GIL; workers give parallelism across cores. More of one never fixes the other.
  • ⚠️ Don't size lifespan pools as if global.
    ↳ Why: a pool of 20 is 20 × workers × pods against the database.
  • ⚠️ Don't put heavy work in BackgroundTasks.
    ↳ Why: it runs on the same loop after the response; queue it (queues).
  • ⚠️ Don't serve CPU-bound inference from the ASGI worker.
    ↳ Why: the GIL still applies; use a separate inference service or a process pool.
  • 🔖 Version: lifespan replaced @app.on_event (deprecated); uvicorn manages --workers natively; anyio's default thread limit is 40.
    ↳ Note: checked with FastAPI 0.142.2, Starlette 1.7.0, CPython 3.12.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: async execution model ─▶ ASGI & workers ─▶ streaming transport ─▶ connection pooling

  • Builds on the event loop: ASGI rides it, so blocking and cancellation rules transfer directly.
  • Builds on the GIL: one worker is one core of real throughput.
  • Used by streaming transport: SSE and WebSockets are sequences of ASGI messages.
  • Breaks when combined with connection pooling: every per-worker pool multiplies by the worker count.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Node runs one event loop per process and scales with a cluster of processes, the same worker math.

notes.title: Reliability Mechanics (Retries · Timeouts · Backoff + Jitter · Circuit Breakers)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Tenacity docs · 📘 HTTPX: timeouts · 📘 pybreaker · 📖 AWS Builders' Library: timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

⚡ TL;DR

Timeouts bound one attempt; retries with backoff + jitter recover from transient failures; a circuit breaker stops retries from amplifying an outage. Classification is the whole game: retry timeouts, 429 and 5xx; never retry deterministic 4xx or an unkeyed mutation.

🧭 Flow: call with per-phase timeouts ─▶ deterministic 4xx? fail now ─▶ breaker open? fail fast or fail over ─▶ transient failure: wait initial·2ⁿ + jitter, retry ─▶ N consecutive failures open the breaker ─▶ after a cooldown one probe decides: close or stay open

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
The four httpx timeouts? connect, read, write, pool, each with its own exception; streaming LLM calls trip read.
Why jitter on backoff? Clients that failed together retry together; randomness de-correlates the waves.
What must never be retried? Deterministic 4xx (400/401/403/404/422), and mutations without an idempotency key.
Breaker states? Closed (counting) ─▶ Open (fail fast) ─▶ Half-open (one probe: success closes, failure re-opens).
Retries vs breaker: who protects whom? Retries protect this request; the breaker protects the upstream and your capacity from your retries.
✏️ Draw by hand: the breaker closed ─N failures▶ open ─cooldown▶ half-open ─probe ok▶ closed, ─probe fails▶ open.

💡 The idea

Every LLM, RAG or agent request is a chain of calls to slow-tailed, rate-limited, sometimes-down upstreams. Each tool here encodes a different belief about why a call failed: too slow (timeout), bad luck (retry), bad timing (backoff + jitter), or actually broken (breaker). The dangerous belief is "retries improve reliability": against a down provider, 1 try + 3 retries makes every request four upstream calls, each holding a coroutine and a pool slot through the backoff ladder. And a timeout isn't a failure; it's an unknown outcome: the charge may have landed after you stopped listening.

The trade: retries turn transient failures into successes, and in exchange they multiply load during real outages, so they need classification, jitter, budgets and a breaker above them.

⚙️ How it works

The breaker is shared state per upstream, per worker:

Rule What actually happens
Timeouts are cancellation httpx arms per-phase timers; asyncio.timeout() throws CancelledError at the suspension point, so timeout handling and cancellation correctness are one skill.
Tenacity's loop AsyncRetrying yields attempts; an exception matching retry= is swallowed, wait= computes a non-blocking asyncio.sleep, stop= ends it; reraise=True surfaces the real error.
The jitter formula wait_exponential_jitter(initial, max) is min(initial·2ⁿ + uniform(0, 1), max); "full jitter", uniform(0, initial·2ⁿ), de-correlates further at a longer expected wait.
Open = fail fast Every call raises immediately with no upstream call: the 4× retry multiplier becomes ~0×, and the open state can drive failover routing.

💻 Code

import httpx
from tenacity import (AsyncRetrying, stop_after_attempt,
                      wait_exponential_jitter, retry_if_exception_type)

class Retryable(Exception):
    """Transient upstream failure: worth another attempt."""

async def call_llm(client: httpx.AsyncClient, url: str, payload: dict) -> dict:
    async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(
        stop=stop_after_attempt(4),                         # 1 try + 3 retries
        wait=wait_exponential_jitter(initial=0.5, max=8),   # 0.5·2ⁿ + uniform(0, 1), capped
        retry=retry_if_exception_type((Retryable, httpx.TimeoutException)),
        reraise=True,                                       # callers see the real error
    ):
        with attempt:
            r = await client.post(url, json=payload)       # the client carries per-phase timeouts
            if r.status_code in (429, 500, 502, 503):
                raise Retryable(f"upstream {r.status_code}")   # transient: retry
            r.raise_for_status()                           # other 4xx: deterministic, never retried
            return r.json()

Against a mock upstream answering 503, 503, 200 (httpx 0.28.1, tenacity 9.1.4, CPython 3.12):

Attempt Started at Upstream What the loop did
1 0.000 s 503 Retryable matched: slept 0.868 s (window 0.5–1.5)
2 0.868 s 503 Retryable matched: slept 1.198 s (window 1–2)
3 2.066 s 200 returned {'text': 'ok'}
control 0.000 s 401 HTTPStatusError not in the predicate: raised after 1 attempt

The allowlist is explicit, never except Exception, so a bug can't be "retried away"; and the sleeps are non-blocking, so hundreds of ladders cost the loop nothing.

⚠️ Break it: retries during a real outage.

# Provider down for 5 minutes. Inbound: 200 req/s. Policy: 1 try + 3 retries, no breaker.
upstream_calls_per_s = 200 * 4            # every request now makes 4 calls
in_flight = 200 * (4 * 6 + 0.5 + 1 + 2)   # 4 read timeouts of 6 s + backoff: ~27.5 s held
# look for: who is hurting whom
# naive model predicts: retries make the gateway more reliable during the outage

800 calls/s hit a provider that's already down, and ~5,500 requests sit in flight holding coroutines and pool slots until your own pool is exhausted and healthy routes time out too. Their incident becomes yours. Fixes by leverage: a breaker per provider, a retry budget (≤10% of volume), and the caller's deadline bounding the whole ladder.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: It's the ordered toolkit around any unreliable call. Timeouts first: an unbounded wait is a leaked resource, and httpx separates connect, read, write and pool. Then retries, only for transient failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff plus jitter, because synchronized retries come back as a thundering herd. A circuit breaker sits above: after N consecutive failures it fails fast so retries can't pile onto a broken upstream, and half-open probes detect recovery.

Q · Mechanism — What does wait_exponential_jitter compute, and why do full-jitter variants exist? min(initial × 2ⁿ + uniform(0, jitter), max) for retry n: a doubling ladder (0.5, 1, 2, 4 s…) plus a random term, capped. The exponential part means a struggling upstream sees geometrically less pressure per client; the cap bounds the tail; the jitter breaks synchronization. Without it, every client that failed in the same instant comes back in the same instant, wave after wave, exactly when the upstream is weakest. Full jitter, uniform(0, initial × 2ⁿ), trades longer waits for maximal de-correlation.

Q · Failure — A provider has a 5-minute outage and you retry 3 times. How does that make it worse? Each request becomes four upstream calls against a provider that's down, and each holds its coroutine, pool slot and memory for the full ladder (see Break it), so in-flight work stacks up until your own pool starves healthy routes. Fixes: a per-provider breaker (open converts 4× to ~0× and drives failover), a retry budget, deadline propagation so no retry starts without budget left, and honouring Retry-After. Also check the SDK isn't retrying underneath you: 3 × 3 × 3 is 27 attempts.

Q · Design — Reliability for an LLM gateway calling 3 providers with a 10 s end-to-end SLO. Work backwards from the deadline: ~1 s for our overhead leaves ~9 s upstream. The first attempt gets connect=2, read=6; for streaming, read bounds time-to-first-token. That leaves room for one retry or one failover. Composition: the deadline wraps everything, failover logic sits outside the breakers, and each provider's breaker (5 failures → open 30 s, one probe) counts transport errors and 5xx, never 4xx or client cancellations. I'd watch retries scheduled past the caller's remaining budget first: billed tokens nobody reads.

⚖️ Compare

Mechanism Protects Acts on Assumes Cost when wrong
Timeout your resources one attempt slow = failed kills legitimately slow calls
Retry this request the next attempt failure is transient amplifies deterministic failures
Backoff + jitter the upstream the schedule recovery needs time and de-correlation adds latency to quick recoveries
Circuit breaker upstream + your capacity all future calls failure is systemic a false open rejects healthy traffic

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Retries improve reliability"
    ✅ Only for transient failures under low contention; against a down upstream they amplify the outage.
  • 🪞 "A timeout means the operation failed"
    ✅ It means the outcome is unknown.
    ↳ So: retrying a mutation without an idempotency key is how duplicate charges happen.
  • 🔀 Not the same: backoff vs jitter
    ↳ Difference: backoff sets how much pressure one client applies; jitter sets whether clients apply it at once.
  • ⚠️ Don't stack retry layers.
    ↳ Why: SDK × app × mesh retries multiply; own the policy at exactly one layer.
  • ⚠️ Don't share one breaker across unrelated endpoints.
    ↳ Why: one flaky endpoint blackholes the healthy ones; breaker granularity = failure-domain granularity.
  • ⚠️ Don't time.sleep for backoff in async code.
    ↳ Why: it blocks every task on the loop; asyncio.sleep is free.
  • 🔖 Version: httpx's default is 5 s on every phase; pybreaker defaults to fail_max=5, reset_timeout=60; asyncio.timeout() is 3.11+.
    ↳ Note: checked with httpx 0.28.1, tenacity 9.1.4, pybreaker 1.4.1; provider SDKs ship their own retry defaults, so re-check them.

🕸️ Connections

Path: cancellation ─▶ reliability mechanics ─▶ idempotency ─▶ rate limiting

  • Builds on tasks & cancellation: timeouts are cancellation, backoff is a non-blocking sleep.
  • Builds on custom exceptions: retry predicates classify by exception type and retryable.
  • Breaks when combined with non-idempotent mutations: a retried timeout can apply twice.
  • Contrasts with queues: for deferrable work, a durable queue beats a synchronous retry ladder.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Envoy and Istio implement retries and outlier detection at the mesh layer; pick one owner per policy.

notes.title: Idempotency (Keys · At-Least-Once vs Exactly-Once · Safe Retries)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Stripe API: idempotent requests · 📜 IETF draft: Idempotency-Key header · 📖 Stripe engineering: designing robust APIs with idempotency

⚡ TL;DR

A timeout is an unknown outcome, so a retried mutation can run twice; an idempotency key makes the retry safe. The server atomically claims the key, runs the side effect once, stores the response, and replays it for every retry.

🧭 Flow: client sends one key per logical operation ─▶ record exists? fingerprint matches: replay; differs: 422 ─▶ no record: atomic claim (SET NX or a unique insert) ─▶ lost the claim: 409, retry later ─▶ won: execute once ─▶ store fingerprint + response with a TTL

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Idempotent, in one line? Doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once: f(f(x)) = f(x).
Which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition? GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS. POST and PATCH aren't, hence the key.
What does the server store under a key? A fingerprint of the request and the first response, replayed on retry.
Why is a timeout the whole motivation? The operation may have succeeded after you stopped listening; only a key makes retrying safe.
Exactly-once delivery: real? No. "Exactly-once" is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
✏️ Draw by hand: the protocol key ─▶ record? ─yes▶ fingerprint match? replay : 422 ─no▶ claim? ─lost▶ 409 ─won▶ execute ─▶ store.

💡 The idea

Retries are only safe on operations that can run twice. The dangerous case is a read timeout on a charge:

Without the key, the retry is indistinguishable from a new charge. "Check whether the charge exists, then create" doesn't fix it: two concurrent retries both check, both find nothing, both create. The claim must be atomic, and the key must be bound to the request body, or a client reusing key abc for a different charge silently gets the old response back.

The trade: one extra store round-trip on every mutation buys the right to retry, and in exchange the store becomes part of the write path, with its own retention and failure policy.

⚙️ How it works

The server protocol (markers match the Code section):

Rule What actually happens
Delivery semantics At-most-once loses messages; at-least-once duplicates them when an ack is lost. Systems that care pick at-least-once and dedup at the receiver: exactly-once effect.
Key scope One key per logical operation, minted at the intent boundary. A fresh UUID per attempt makes the whole layer decorative.
Shared store The claim must live in Redis or the database: an in-process lock doesn't survive multiple workers.
Retention At least the longest retry horizon, including queue redelivery; Stripe keeps keys about 24 h.

💻 Code

import hashlib, json
from redis.asyncio import Redis

def fingerprint(params: dict) -> str:
    # sort_keys: {'a': 1, 'b': 2} and {'b': 2, 'a': 1} hash the same
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(params, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

async def idempotent_charge(redis: Redis, key: str, params: dict) -> dict:
    if (stored := await redis.get(f"idem:{key}")):              # ① record exists?
        rec = json.loads(stored)
        if rec["fp"] != fingerprint(params):
            raise ValueError("422: key reused with different params")   # a client bug
        return rec["response"]                                   #   replay: no side effect
    if not await redis.set(f"idem:{key}:lock", "1", nx=True, ex=30):    # ② atomic claim
        raise RuntimeError("409: original still in flight; retry later")
    try:
        response = await do_charge(params)                       # ③ exactly once
        await redis.set(f"idem:{key}",                            # ④ store for replay
                        json.dumps({"fp": fingerprint(params), "response": response}),
                        ex=86400)
        return response
    finally:
        await redis.delete(f"idem:{key}:lock")    # a transient failure frees the key for a retry

Run with fakeredis on CPython 3.12, params = {"amount": 4999, "currency": "inr", "customer": "cus_42"}: the first call charged ch_0001; a retry with the same params in a different key order replayed ch_0001 with charges still at 1; amount: 9999 under the same key raised the 422; two concurrent calls on a fresh key produced one ch_0002 and one 409. The stored record's TTL read 86400.

⚠️ Break it: the crash between execute and store.

response = await do_charge(params)   # ③ the provider commits the charge
# ── worker is OOM-killed here: the finally never runs; the lock expires after 30 s ──
await redis.set(f"idem:{key}", ...)  # ④ never happens
# look for: what the next retry with the same key finds
# naive model predicts: the key layer guarantees one charge

The retry finds no record and an expired lock, so it charges again: the exact duplicate the layer exists to prevent. Two writes to two systems can't be atomic. If the side effect is in your database, insert the key record and the charge row in one transaction. If it's external, store the key as in_progress before calling, pass the same key to the provider (Stripe dedups it), and on retry reconcile by asking the provider what happened instead of executing again.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Idempotency makes retries safe. A timeout means the outcome is unknown, so a blind retry might charge or write twice. The client sends one key per logical operation; the server atomically claims it, runs the side effect once, stores the response and replays it for every retry, rejecting the same key with a different body. Delivery stays at-least-once; idempotent processing makes the effect exactly-once.

Q · Mechanism — At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: where does idempotency sit? At-most-once never retries, so nothing duplicates but losses are permanent: fine for metrics. At-least-once retries until acknowledged, so nothing is lost, but every lost ack produces a duplicate. Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network isn't achievable, because a receiver can't tell a new message from a retry without state. What is achievable is exactly-once processing: at-least-once delivery plus dedup by key, or the effect and the processed-key record written in one transaction. Kafka's EOS is that construction.

Q · Failure — The layer stores the response after the charge succeeds, and a worker crashes in between. What happens? The retry finds no record and re-executes: a duplicate (see Break it). The fix depends on where the effect lives: one transaction for local effects, so the crash rolls back both; for external effects, record in_progress first, propagate the key downstream, and reconcile on retry by querying the provider. Alert on lease-expiry re-executions, which should be ~0.

Q · Design — Idempotency for an agent runtime whose LLM tool calls (payments, emails, tickets) are retried by the reliability layer. Mint keys at the intent boundary, deterministically: run_id:step_id:tool:params_hash, so any replay of that step regenerates the same key. Every side-effecting tool goes through the protocol above against a shared store, and keys propagate to providers that accept them. What breaks: fingerprint drift when the model rewords a memo (normalize what you hash), two workers claiming one step (the claim must be in the shared store), and replaying stored transient errors forever (store only deterministic failures).

⚖️ Compare

Semantics Mechanism Loses data? Duplicates? Use when
At-most-once send, never retry yes no metrics, best-effort telemetry
At-least-once retry until ack no yes the default for anything that matters
"Exactly-once" at-least-once + idempotent processing no effect happens once payments, orders, any non-idempotent effect

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "My queue supports exactly-once delivery"
    ✅ A lost ack is indistinguishable from a lost message; what you get is at-least-once plus idempotent processing.
  • 🪞 "Retrying is safe if the timeout was short"
    ✅ A read timeout means the server was mid-work: the charge may have committed. Safety comes from the key, never from probability.
  • 🔀 Not the same as caching
    ↳ Difference: a cache may miss harmlessly; an idempotency record must not miss within its window, or a side effect repeats.
  • ⚠️ Don't key naturally idempotent operations.
    ↳ Why: GET, full-state PUT and upserts already tolerate repeats; the store round-trip buys nothing.
  • ⚠️ Don't let the store fail open by default.
    ↳ Why: the day Redis blips is the day duplicates ship; for payments, fail closed, and choose explicitly.
  • 🔖 Version: Idempotency-Key is an IETF draft, not an RFC; retention and mismatch behaviour are per provider.
    ↳ Note: the trace ran on CPython 3.12.13 with fakeredis.

🕸️ Connections

Path: reliability mechanics ─▶ idempotency ─▶ queues & workers

  • Builds on reliability mechanics: this is what makes retrying a mutation safe.
  • Used by queues & workers: at-least-once redelivery needs idempotent consumers.
  • Contrasts with caching: the same lookup shape with the opposite miss tolerance.
  • Used by structured logging: log the key on every attempt; it's the correlation ID for duplicates.
  • Same idea elsewhere: AWS ClientToken on mutating APIs and SQS FIFO deduplication IDs are the same contract.

notes.title: Rate Limiting (Token Bucket · Sliding Window · Where to Enforce)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Redis: build 5 rate limiters · 📘 Redis glossary: rate limiting

⚡ TL;DR

A token bucket refills at rate per second up to capacity; each request spends tokens: a steady rate with bounded bursts, in O(1). Limiter state must be shared and atomic across workers, and provider limits are a budget to schedule, not an error to retry.

🧭 Flow: allow(cost) ─▶ lazy refill: tokens += elapsed × rate, capped at capacity ─▶ enough tokens? spend them and admit ─▶ not enough: 429, or a bounded queue ─▶ across workers, the same two fields live in Redis behind one atomic Lua step

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Token bucket in one line? Refill at rate up to capacity; spend per request: long-run rate plus bounded bursts.
Fixed window's flaw, and the fix? 2× the limit straddling a window edge; a sliding window counts over a rolling interval.
The three enforcement points? Gateway (protect yourself), client-side (stay inside a provider's quota), and honouring the provider's own 429s.

💡 The idea

Real traffic is bursty, so the useful guarantee is a long-run rate plus a bounded burst, and a token bucket gives exactly that with two numbers per key. On CPython 3.12, TokenBucket(rate=10, capacity=20) admitted 20 of 30 immediate requests (the burst budget), then, after a 0.5 s pause, 5 more (0.5 s × 10/s). There's no timer thread: refill is computed lazily on each call from time.monotonic(). The architect question is where: a "100 RPS" bucket kept in each process of 4 workers × 30 pods allows 12,000 RPS in total, and the read-modify-write races over-admit under exactly the load you built it for.

The trade: a limiter says "no" cheaply at the edge, and in exchange it needs shared, atomic state, and it bounds traffic without smoothing it.

⚙️ How it works

Rule What actually happens
Capacity vs rate Capacity is the burst budget (the bucket starts full); rate is sustained throughput.
Fixed window INCR + EXPIRE per calendar minute: 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01 are 200 requests in two seconds, all "within limit".
Sliding window Exact as a timestamp log (a sorted set: memory per request), or approximate as a weighted pair of counters (O(1)).
Distributed Tokens and last-refill live in a Redis hash; refill-check-spend runs as one Lua script using Redis server time, so 120 workers can't race.
Provider-facing A client-side bucket sized to the contracted quota (requests and tokens per minute for LLMs) queues or sheds before the wire.

💻 Code

import time

class TokenBucket:
    """rate = sustained tokens/s; capacity = burst budget. One instance per key."""
    def __init__(self, rate: float, capacity: float):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.tokens, self.updated = capacity, time.monotonic()   # start full: burst allowed

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1.0) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()                                   # immune to NTP clock steps
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.updated) * self.rate)
        self.updated = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost              # cost > 1: weighted work, e.g. LLM tokens
            return True
        return False                         # the caller returns 429, or queues with a bound

The cost parameter is the LLM-relevant detail: provider budgets are tokens per minute, so a request's cost is its estimated token count, not 1. In-process, this class is a useful pre-filter that sheds obvious overload before a Redis round-trip; the authoritative check stays shared.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Rate limiting bounds request rate to protect a resource. The token bucket is the workhorse: tokens refill steadily up to a capacity and each request spends one, giving a long-run rate plus controlled bursts in O(1) with two numbers of state. A sliding window counts over a rolling interval, fixing the fixed-window boundary burst. Then placement: at the gateway to protect yourself, shared in Redis; and client-side to stay inside each provider's quota.

Q · Mechanism — 4 workers × 30 pods: where does limiter state live, and how do you handle provider 429s? Per-worker state multiplies the limit by 120 and races, so the authoritative bucket lives in Redis with refill-check-spend as one atomic Lua step; local buckets only pre-filter. Provider-facing is inverted: the provider enforces and you comply. Treating 429 as transient and retrying presses harder on an exhausted quota. Instead, run a client-side bucket sized to RPM and TPM, honour Retry-After, and make backpressure explicit with a bounded queue.

⚖️ Compare

Algorithm State per key Bursts Accuracy Cost
Token bucket two floats allowed up to capacity exact long-run rate O(1)
Fixed window one counter 2× at boundaries rough O(1), cheapest
Sliding window log a timestamp per request none exact O(log n) + memory
Sliding window counter two counters mostly smoothed approximate O(1)

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A rate limiter smooths traffic"
    ✅ It bounds traffic; admitted requests stay as bursty as they arrived.
    ↳ Smoothing is shaping: a queue that delays, paid for in memory and latency.
  • 🔀 Not the same as backpressure
    ↳ Difference: rate limiting is an admission decision at the edge; backpressure is a flow signal slowing producers (bounded queues). You need both.
  • ⚠️ Don't keep limiter state in-process across workers.
    ↳ Why: the limit multiplies by instance count and races over-admit.
  • ⚠️ Don't queue unboundedly behind a limiter.
    ↳ Why: that just moves the flood into your memory.
  • ⚠️ Don't use a sliding-window log on hot keys at high QPS.
    ↳ Why: memory per request per window becomes a Redis memory incident; use two counters.
  • 🔖 Version: use time.monotonic() locally and Redis server time in Lua; LLM providers limit RPM and TPM per model and tier, so verify per contract.
    ↳ Note: the bucket numbers were measured on CPython 3.12.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: async primitives ─▶ rate limiting ─▶ reliability mechanics

  • Builds on the worker model: per-worker state multiplies the limit.
  • Contrasts with retries: compliant clients don't retry into an exhausted quota.
  • Same mechanism as caching: the same Redis counters and TTLs, used to say no cheaply instead of yes.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Nginx limit_req and Envoy's local and global rate limits implement the same bucket at the proxy.

notes.title: Streaming Transport (SSE vs WebSocket · Async Generators as Producer · Backpressure · Mid-Stream Cancellation)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 HTML Standard: server-sent events · 📜 PEP 525: asynchronous generators · 📘 Starlette: responses · 📘 FastAPI: WebSockets

⚡ TL;DR

SSE is the default for LLM tokens: one-way, plain HTTP, auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID; WebSocket only when the client must talk mid-stream. An async generator behind StreamingResponse is pull-based, so a slow client paces it for free, and a disconnect cancels it into its finally.

🧭 Flow: StreamingResponse pulls __anext__ ─▶ generator resumes at yield, produces one chunk ─▶ ASGI send() ─▶ full TCP buffer? send() waits and the generator stays paused ─▶ client disconnects: the server cancels the task ─▶ CancelledError at the current await ─▶ finally closes the upstream stream

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
SSE vs WebSocket, one line each? SSE: one-way over plain HTTP, reconnect built in. WebSocket: full duplex after an upgrade; reconnect is your problem.
Why is an async generator the natural producer? It's pull-based: each __anext__ makes one chunk, so a slow consumer paces it.
What happens to the generator on disconnect? The server cancels the task; CancelledError lands at its current await, and finally runs.
SSE's reconnection contract? The client reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID; resuming from it is your job.
The interrupt button: WebSocket? No: an interrupt is one message; a plain POST …/cancel does it.
✏️ Draw by hand: the pull loop pull ─▶ resume at yield ─▶ chunk ─▶ send ─▶ TCP buffer ─▶ next pull; disconnect ─▶ cancel ─▶ finally.

💡 The idea

Time to first token is what users feel, so every LLM product streams, and the cheap, correct producer is an async generator. Nothing drives it ahead of the client: each chunk exists only because the transport pulled it. Measured with FastAPI 0.142.2 on CPython 3.12, five tokens 50 ms apart, driving the ASGI app directly:

Consumer Tokens produced at Total
fast 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.21, 0.26 s 0.256 s
slow (each send takes 0.2 s) 0.05, 0.30, 0.55, 0.81, 1.06 s 1.462 s
disconnects after 2 chunks (uvicorn's ASGI 2.3 path) 0.05, 0.10 s; then CancelledError in the generator 0.128 s

The slow consumer stretched production to its own pace with no code for it: that's backpressure. The disconnected client got two chunks and the other three were never generated, which is the money: with a real provider, finally closing the upstream stream is what stops tokens being billed.

The trade: a pull-based generator gives backpressure and cancellation for free, and in exchange cleanup must live in finally, and anything that buffers or swallows CancelledError silently breaks both.

⚙️ How it works

The pull loop, and the disconnect edge (markers match the Code section):

Rule What actually happens
One paused frame per stream A PEP 525 generator between chunks is a suspended frame holding its locals: KB-scale, which is the 50K-streams-per-box economics (coroutines).
Backpressure location async for chunk in gen plus send() awaiting the server's flow control. Nothing pulls faster than the slowest link.
Cancellation rides the task uvicorn reports disconnect through receive; Starlette cancels the streaming task, so CancelledError lands at the generator's current await (cancellation).
SSE wire format data: lines and a blank line per event; id: enables resume; : ping comment lines are heartbeats that keep proxies from idling out.

💻 Code

import asyncio, json
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()

async def token_stream(upstream, prompt: str):
    """Pull-based SSE producer: a slow client pauses this frame at `yield`."""
    try:
        i = 0
        async for tok in upstream.stream(prompt):          # ① one pull, one token
            yield f"id: {i}\ndata: {json.dumps({'token': tok})}\n\n"   # id: enables resume
            i += 1
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    finally:                                               # ② normal end AND disconnect
        await upstream.aclose()                            # ③ or the provider keeps billing

@app.post("/stream")
async def stream(request: Request, prompt: str):
    return StreamingResponse(
        token_stream(request.app.state.llm, prompt),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"},  # nginx: don't buffer
    )

Two load-bearing choices: the producer is a generator (pull, so backpressure) rather than a task filling a queue (push, so an unbounded buffer), and cleanup lives in finally, because cancellation arrives as an exception at a suspension point, not as a callback.

⚠️ Break it: the push shape people build by accident.

async def stream_push(prompt):
    q = asyncio.Queue()                                   # ❌ unbounded
    async def pump():
        async for tok in upstream.stream(prompt):
            await q.put(tok)                              # never waits: runs at model speed
    asyncio.create_task(pump())                           # ❌ not tied to the response's lifetime
    while (tok := await q.get()) is not None:
        yield f"data: {tok}\n\n"
# look for: a slow client, then a client that disconnects
# naive model predicts: same behaviour as the generator, just "decoupled"

A slow reader turns the queue into RSS growth (the OOM signature); a disconnect cancels the response but not the detached pump task, which keeps the provider generating tokens nobody reads. If producer and delivery must decouple (fan-out, cross-worker handoff), bound the queue so put() waits (bounded queues) and cancel the producer in finally.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Two production options. SSE: one-way text/event-stream over plain HTTP, auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID, passes through every proxy. WebSocket: full duplex after an upgrade, for clients that talk mid-stream. In Python the producer is an async generator behind StreamingResponse: pull-based, so each chunk is produced only when the transport is ready, and a disconnect cancels the task so finally can close the upstream call.

Q · Mechanism — How does an async generator behind StreamingResponse pace itself to a slow client? Nothing drives it ahead. StreamingResponse runs async for chunk in gen: each iteration resumes the frame at its last yield, runs to the next, and hands the chunk to ASGI send(). That send participates in the server's flow control; when the TCP send buffer is full because the client reads slowly, it waits, so the loop waits, so the generator stays paused. Measured: a 0.2 s consumer stretched five 50 ms tokens to 1.46 s. You create a backpressure problem by adding an unbounded queue.

Q · Failure — Streams freeze at ~60 s, and the token bill exceeds delivered tokens. Two bugs. The freeze is infrastructure: a hop with an idle timeout (nginx proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 s, ALBs have their own) kills the quiet connection during a long tool call. Fix with heartbeat comments under the timeout and X-Accel-Buffering: no. The bill gap is cancellation leakage: clients disconnect, but the upstream keeps generating because finally doesn't close it, a detached task produces (see Break it), or code swallows CancelledError. Track wasted tokens: generated minus delivered.

Q · Design — 50K concurrent streams, browser and mobile clients, user interrupts, deploys mid-conversation. SSE for tokens and a plain POST /cancel for interrupts, avoiding WebSocket's upgrade, stickiness and reconnect tax. 50K streams is asyncio's home ground across a handful of workers. Deploys force resumability: monotonic event IDs, each generation's events buffered in Redis for minutes, replay from Last-Event-ID on reconnect. I'd watch wasted-token ratio, time-to-first-token p99 per provider, open streams per worker, and reconnect rate.

⚖️ Compare

Long polling SSE WebSocket
Direction client pulls, server holds server → client full duplex
Transport plain HTTP plain HTTP, text/event-stream HTTP 101 upgrade, framed TCP
Reconnect, resume n/a built in + Last-Event-ID build it yourself
Proxy, LB friction timeouts low: buffering and idle timeouts high: upgrade support, stickiness
LLM fit legacy fallback ✅ the token-streaming default interrupts in-band, voice, collaboration

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "WebSocket is modern, SSE is legacy"
    ✅ They're different tools: every major LLM API streams over SSE-style chunked HTTP.
  • 🪞 "I need to implement backpressure for my SSE endpoint"
    ✅ A generator producer already has it; you create the problem by adding an unbounded queue.
  • 🔀 Not the same: client disconnected vs producer stopped
    ↳ Difference: they're joined only by cancellation propagating correctly: finally must close the upstream, and nothing may swallow CancelledError.
  • ⚠️ Don't stream through middleware that reads the body.
    ↳ Why: it buffers the whole stream (measured in 73).
  • ⚠️ Don't hold a DB connection across the stream.
    ↳ Why: it's pinned for minutes, so a 20-slot pool serves 20 users (pooling). Fetch, release, then stream.
  • ⚠️ Don't ship without heartbeats and event IDs.
    ↳ Why: idle timeouts sever long generations, and retrofitting IDs is a protocol change for every client.
  • 🔖 Version: async generators 3.6+ (PEP 525); CancelledError is a BaseException since 3.8. Starlette cancels the stream on disconnect under ASGI spec < 2.4 (uvicorn 0.54 reports 2.3); under 2.4 a failed send ends it and the generator's finally runs only when it's finalized, ~10 ms later in the test.
    ↳ Note: checked with FastAPI 0.142.2, Starlette 1.7.0, uvicorn 0.54.0.

🕸️ Connections

Path: cancellation ─▶ ASGI ─▶ streaming transport ─▶ connection pooling

  • Builds on generators: the same lazy pull, made async by PEP 525.
  • Builds on tasks & cancellation: how CancelledError reaches the paused frame.
  • Used by the ASGI worker: each yield is one http.response.body message.
  • Breaks when combined with connection pools: a resource held across a stream is held for minutes.
  • Same idea elsewhere: HTTP/2 and gRPC server streaming use flow-control windows for the same pull-paced backpressure.

notes.title: Connection Pooling from Async Code
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 asyncpg: connection pools · 📘 SQLAlchemy 2: connection pooling · 📘 PgBouncer features

⚡ TL;DR

A pool is a bounded set of warm connections with checkout and checkin; it amortizes the TCP + TLS + auth handshake and keeps you under Postgres's max_connections. Async pools are small: size to concurrent in-flight queries, then multiply by workers and pods.

🧭 Flow: pool.acquire() ─▶ a free connection? use it ─▶ none, under max_size? dial one (pay the handshake) ─▶ at max: the coroutine waits in the pool's queue ─▶ released in time? use it; else TimeoutError ─▶ async with exit returns it to the pool

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Why pool at all? A new connection is TCP + TLS + auth, tens of ms; Postgres caps max_connections (default 100) and each backend costs server RAM.
The async sizing rule? Concurrent in-flight queries, not requests: connections come back between queries. 10–20 per worker often serves thousands of requests.
A sync driver inside a coroutine? psycopg2 blocks the loop's only thread; every task stalls for the query's duration.

💡 The idea

Size from the database, not the app. Postgres's max_connections is a budget shared by every instance, plus migrations, admin and replication, and past a couple of hundred active connections the server degrades rather than speeds up. Sync services need about workers × threads per pod, because a thread pins its connection for the whole handler. Async services need far fewer, because each query holds a connection only while it runs. Then the multiplication bites: a pool of 20 in lifespan is per worker, so 4 workers × 30 pods × 20 is 2,400 connections against a cap of 100. When that can't fit, an external pooler (PgBouncer) multiplexes many client connections onto few server ones.

The trade: warm, bounded connections make queries cheap and protect the database, and in exchange the pool becomes a queue that every request can end up waiting in.

⚙️ How it works

Rule What actually happens
Waiting is async-native An async pool parks the coroutine and the loop keeps serving others; a sync pool blocks the OS thread.
Two different timeouts In asyncpg 0.31, create_pool has no acquire timeout: extra keywords go to connect() (establishment, default 60 s). Waiting is bounded by pool.acquire(timeout=…).
SQLAlchemy async create_async_engine picked AsyncAdaptedQueuePool (SQLAlchemy 2.1.2); the default QueuePool uses a thread lock and isn't asyncio-safe.
PgBouncer transaction mode Breaks session state (prepared statements, LISTEN/NOTIFY, SET); asyncpg behind it needs statement_cache_size=0.

💻 Code

import asyncpg
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, Request

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(
        dsn="postgresql://app:secret@db:5432/app",
        min_size=5,                              # pre-warm: absorb the startup spike
        max_size=20,                             # per WORKER: multiplies by --workers
        max_inactive_connection_lifetime=300,    # recycle idle connections after 5 min
        command_timeout=30,                      # a runaway query can't pin a connection
        server_settings={"application_name": "llm-gateway"},  # findable in pg_stat_activity
    )
    yield
    await app.state.pool.close()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

async def get_conn(request: Request):
    async with request.app.state.pool.acquire(timeout=10) as conn:   # the ACQUIRE timeout
        yield conn                                                   # released on exit

@app.get("/candidates/{cid}")
async def get_candidate(cid: str, conn: asyncpg.Connection = Depends(get_conn)):
    row = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT id, name FROM candidates WHERE id = $1", cid)
    return dict(row) if row else None

command_timeout is the anti-pinning guard and application_name is for incident response: it's how you find your connections in pg_stat_activity at 3 am.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A pool keeps a bounded set of warm connections with checkout and checkin, amortizing the tens-of-ms handshake and keeping the app under Postgres's max_connections. Sizing is the senior point: sync needs about workers × threads, because a thread holds its connection for the whole handler; async pools are much smaller, because connections return between queries. And every per-worker pool multiplies by workers and pods, which is when PgBouncer comes in.

Q · Mechanism — p99 jumps from 20 ms to 10 s under load; CPU is low; pg_stat_activity shows 20 busy connections. Walk through it. Twenty busy on a max_size=20 pool means every further acquire() waits in the pool's queue: requests aren't slow, they're queued, the p99-cliff-with-idle-CPU signature. Raising max_size rarely fixes it. Find what holds the connections: a slow query (old state_change), a transaction held open across an LLM call (pinned for the provider's tail), a stream holding one for minutes, or N+1 queries. Alert on pool saturation above 0.8 and set an acquire timeout so overload fails fast.

⚖️ Compare

In-process pool (asyncpg, SQLAlchemy) External pooler (PgBouncer)
Scope per worker process shared across pods and services
When workers × pods × pool fits under the cap many pods, serverless, many services
Cost nothing extra one more hop; transaction mode breaks session features

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Bigger pool = more throughput"
    ✅ Connections are a server-bounded, shared resource; hundreds of active ones degrade Postgres.
  • 🪞 "Async needs a big pool: look at my concurrent requests"
    ✅ Backwards: size to queries actually executing, often 1–2 orders of magnitude below request count.
  • ⚠️ Don't run sync drivers inside async def.
    ↳ Why: the query blocks the loop; use asyncpg, async psycopg or AsyncEngine, or to_thread as a stopgap (bridging).
  • ⚠️ Don't hold a transaction across slow awaits.
    ↳ Why: async with conn.transaction(): around an LLM call pins the connection for the provider's tail; do the slow work first.
  • ⚠️ Don't pool per invocation in serverless.
    ↳ Why: hundreds of fresh processes each dialing blow max_connections in seconds; use an external pooler.
  • ⚠️ Don't tune the pool when the disease is N+1.
    ↳ Why: 50 queries per request exhaust any pool; fix the access pattern.

🕸️ Connections

Path: context managers ─▶ ASGI workers ─▶ connection pooling ─▶ reliability mechanics

  • Builds on context managers: checkout and checkin is the canonical async with.
  • Builds on the worker model: lifespan owns the pool, once per worker.
  • Breaks when combined with streaming: a connection held across a stream is held for minutes.
  • Same mechanism as rate limiting: a bounded resource with the same queue-or-reject decision.
  • Same idea elsewhere: HikariCP in Java is sized by the same rule: connections ≈ concurrent queries, far below thread count.

notes.title: Caching Patterns (lru_cache · TTL · Redis-backed · Stampedes)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 functools: lru_cache, cache, cached_property · 📘 cachetools · 📖 Real Python: caching with lru_cache

⚡ TL;DR

Caching trades freshness for latency and load: lru_cache in-process, Redis cache-aside across pods, a TTL chosen per entity. A hot key expiring under load stampedes the source unless one caller fetches while the rest wait (single-flight).

🧭 Flow: get(key) ─▶ hit and fresh? return ─▶ miss: take the per-key lock ─▶ re-check the cache (someone may have filled it) ─▶ still missing: fetch from the source once ─▶ SET key EX ttl ─▶ release; the waiters' re-check now hits

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
@lru_cache on a method: what leaks? The key includes self, so the cache pins every instance for its lifetime.
@lru_cache on an async def: what breaks? It caches the coroutine object; the second hit awaits it again: RuntimeError: cannot reuse already awaited coroutine.
A stampede, and the fix? A hot key expires and every concurrent caller hits the source; single-flight lets one fetch while the rest wait and re-check.

💡 The idea

In-process, functools.lru_cache is O(1) memoization: a hash map plus a linked list. Two traps make it wrong for service code. On CPython 3.12, an @lru_cache async def returned 2 once, then raised RuntimeError: cannot reuse already awaited coroutine; and an instance whose method was cached was still alive after del and gc.collect(). Across pods the cache moves to Redis in the cache-aside shape: check, miss, fetch, populate with a TTL, and on writes update the source and delete the key. The incident shape is the stampede: a 30 s leaderboard key expiring under 500 RPS sends 500 identical queries to the database at once, exhausting the pool for unrelated endpoints too.

The trade: a cache shields the source and cuts latency, and in exchange you own staleness, invalidation across pods, and the moment the shield drops.

⚙️ How it works

Single-flight on a cold key (markers match the Code section):

Rule What actually happens
Cache-aside The app owns the logic; Redis down degrades to slow-but-correct if cache errors are treated as misses.
Write-through Writes land in cache and source together: read-after-write consistency, at write latency, with the cache on the write path.
Across pods The in-process lock is per worker; cross-pod single-flight uses Redis SET key 1 NX EX n as a fetch lease.
Refinements Serve stale while one caller refreshes; or probabilistic early refresh, so a hot key never expires for everyone at once.

💻 Code

import asyncio, hashlib, json
from redis.asyncio import Redis

redis = Redis.from_url("redis://cache:6379", decode_responses=True)
_locks: dict[str, asyncio.Lock] = {}          # grows per key: bound it (cachetools.LRUCache)

def _key(text: str, model: str) -> str:
    return f"emb:{model}:{hashlib.sha256(f'{model}:{text}'.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]}"

async def get_embedding(text: str, model: str = "text-embedding-3-small") -> list[float]:
    cache_key = _key(text, model)
    if (cached := await redis.get(cache_key)):            # ① fast path
        return json.loads(cached)
    lock = _locks.setdefault(cache_key, asyncio.Lock())
    async with lock:                                      # ② one fetcher per key per worker
        if (cached := await redis.get(cache_key)):        # ③ double-check: a waiter hits here
            return json.loads(cached)
        embedding = await call_embedding_api(text, model)            # ms and money
        await redis.set(cache_key, json.dumps(embedding), ex=86400)  # TTL fits the DATA
        return embedding

With fakeredis on CPython 3.12, 50 concurrent misses on one key made exactly 1 source call, all 50 callers got the same vector, and the stored TTL read 86400. Embeddings of stable text can live a day; a user profile wants invalidate-on-write; a live price wants seconds.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Caching trades freshness for latency and load. In-process, lru_cache gives O(1) memoization; across pods, Redis cache-aside: check, miss, fetch, populate with a TTL. Three things mark a senior answer: lru_cache pins self on methods and caches coroutine objects on async functions; a hot key expiring under load stampedes the source unless one caller fetches while the others wait; and TTL is a per-entity freshness contract.

Q · Mechanism — A hot key with a 30 s TTL expires under 500 RPS. What happens, and what's the fix? Every reader misses within the same few milliseconds and falls through to the expensive query: 500 identical requests instead of one, the DB pool exhausts, unrelated endpoints sharing it slow down, and if the query is slow the key stays cold while the herd re-piles. Single-flight fixes it: a per-key lock with a double-check after acquiring (1 source call for 50 misses, measured), or a Redis SET NX lease across pods. Then serve stale while refreshing, or refresh early probabilistically.

⚖️ Compare

@lru_cache / @cache cachetools.TTLCache Redis cache-aside
Scope per process (per worker) per process shared across pods
Eviction LRU by count (@cache: unbounded) TTL + size TTL + maxmemory-policy
Cost per hit a dict lookup, ns ns to µs a network hop, ~1 ms
Invalidation cache_clear() only expiry delete, versioned keys, pub/sub
Fits pure functions of immutable args in-process data with a staleness budget anything multi-pod or restart-surviving

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Invalidation is delete(key) on write"
    ✅ Only for one shared cache; with in-process caches on 10 pods, nine keep serving stale until TTL.
    ↳ Fix: a shared cache, pub/sub broadcast, or versioned keys (user:42:v3).
  • 🪞 "Pick a sensible default TTL, say 5 minutes"
    ✅ TTL is a per-entity freshness contract; one default ships the wrong staleness everywhere.
  • 🔀 Not the same as idempotency
    ↳ Difference: a cache miss is free; an idempotency record miss is a duplicate write.
  • ⚠️ Don't @lru_cache async functions or methods.
    ↳ Instead: async-lru or aiocache for coroutines; cached_property or cachetools.cachedmethod per instance.
  • ⚠️ Don't let the cache become a hard dependency.
    ↳ Why: on Redis errors, fall through to the source: an outage should mean slow, never down.
  • ⚠️ Don't cache low-hit-rate personalized data.
    ↳ Why: you pay the lookup for ~0% hits; measure the hit ratio first.
  • 🔖 Version: functools.cache 3.9+ is unbounded; lru_cache defaults to maxsize=128; redis-py's asyncio API is redis.asyncio (aioredis merged in).
    ↳ Note: Redis's default maxmemory-policy is noeviction, which surprises people.

🕸️ Connections

Path: functools ─▶ caching patterns ─▶ reliability mechanics

  • Builds on the functools toolkit: lru_cache and its method leak.
  • Builds on async primitives: per-key locks and the double-check.
  • Contrasts with idempotency: the same lookup shape with the opposite miss tolerance.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: serve stale on error while a breaker is open.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Go's singleflight package and CDN request collapsing are the same single-flight fix.

notes.title: Queues & Background Workers (SQS Consumers · Visibility Timeouts · acks_late · The Poison-Pill Pattern)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Amazon SQS: visibility timeout · 📘 Amazon SQS: dead-letter queues · 📘 Celery: tasks and acknowledgement

⚡ TL;DR

Receive hides a message for the visibility timeout; only delete_message after success acknowledges it, so a crash means redelivery. That's crash recovery for transient faults and a fleet-wide crash loop for a poison message, unless maxReceiveCount parks it in a DLQ.

🧭 Flow: producer sends ─▶ worker receives: message invisible, receive count + 1 ─▶ success: delete_message is the ack ─▶ crash (exit 137, nothing runs): the timeout expires and it's visible again ─▶ count over maxReceiveCount? the broker moves it to the DLQ ─▶ alarm, triage the reproducer

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Why does one poison message kill a whole fleet? Crash before ack means redelivery, so every worker takes its turn dying; maxReceiveCount + DLQ breaks the loop.
What is the "ack" in SQS? delete_message with the receipt handle, after success.
Visibility-timeout sizing rule? Longer than worst-case job time, or heartbeat-extend it; else a slow, live worker's job runs twice.

💡 The idea

Written from a real incident: in the cv-parser, one resume's SQL cartesian product produced 1,295 embeddings instead of ~50–150, the worker was OOM-killed (exit 137: no finally, no cleanup, no delete), the message became visible again, and the next worker died the same way. The fleet was healthy; the message was the pathogen, travelling from worker to worker by redelivery (the memory-side diagnosis). The diagnostic pivot is correlating failures by message ID, not host. Redelivery is the same mechanism in both stories: retry for a transient fault, re-execution of the same bad input for a deterministic one.

The trade: at-least-once delivery means no job is silently lost, and in exchange every handler must be idempotent and every queue needs a cap and a DLQ, or one bad input takes everything down.

⚙️ How it works

One message's lifecycle:

Under moto 5.2.3 with a real boto3 client, VisibilityTimeout=1 and maxReceiveCount=3, a consumer that crashed every time saw:

Time Receive What happened
0.0 s count 1 crash, no delete
1.1 s count 2 visible again after the timeout; crash
2.2 s count 3 crash
3.3 s main queue empty the broker redrove it: the DLQ held {"resume_id": 4711} intact

💻 Code

import json, boto3

sqs = boto3.client("sqs", region_name="us-east-1")
dlq_arn = sqs.get_queue_attributes(QueueUrl=dlq_url, AttributeNames=["QueueArn"])["Attributes"]["QueueArn"]
q = sqs.create_queue(QueueName="parse-jobs", Attributes={
    "VisibilityTimeout": "300",                 # > worst-case job; heartbeat-extend past that
    "RedrivePolicy": json.dumps({               # the poison-pill defense lives in the BROKER
        "deadLetterTargetArn": dlq_arn, "maxReceiveCount": "3"}),
})["QueueUrl"]

def consume_once() -> None:
    msgs = sqs.receive_message(QueueUrl=q, MaxNumberOfMessages=1, WaitTimeSeconds=20,  # long poll
                               AttributeNames=["ApproximateReceiveCount"]).get("Messages", [])
    if not msgs:
        return
    m = msgs[0]
    job = json.loads(m["Body"])
    guard_input_size(job)                       # reject oversized work BEFORE the expensive part
    process_idempotently(job)                   # keyed on message identity: retries never duplicate
    sqs.delete_message(QueueUrl=q, ReceiptHandle=m["ReceiptHandle"])   # the ack, ONLY after success

The DLQ is where the incident starts: the parked message is the reproducer. For the cv-parser it exposed the join fanning out to 1,295 rows, which no retry would ever have fixed. The durable fixes stack: an input-size guard before the expensive work, idempotent processing keyed on the job, and an alarm on DLQ depth with an owner.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A worker queue gives at-least-once delivery: receive hides a message for the visibility timeout, and only an explicit delete after success acknowledges it. Crash before delete and it comes back, which is what you want for transient failures and what melts the fleet when the message itself is the problem. The poison-pill defense is a receive-count cap with a dead-letter queue, plus idempotent handlers, because redelivery guarantees duplicates.

Q · Mechanism — One job crashes every worker that touches it: a rolling OOM-kill. Diagnose and fix. The signature is failures correlating with one message, not a host, deploy or time of day; meanwhile healthy jobs behind it stall. Containment is the broker's job: a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount, so the third strike parks it. Then triage the DLQ body offline as a reproducer. Fix the class: input-size guards before expensive work, idempotent processing, in-job retries with backoff for transient faults (reliability) so receive counts aren't burned on network blips, and alarms on DLQ depth and receive-count distribution.

⚖️ Compare

Raw SQS consumer Celery RQ
Broker SQS (managed) Redis, RabbitMQ or SQS Redis
Ack model explicit delete_message early by default; acks_late=True for crash safety job claimed off a list; worker heartbeats
Poison-pill defense maxReceiveCount + DLQ in the broker max_retries + a failure queue max_retries ─▶ FailedJobRegistry
Wins when AWS-native, minimal deps rich routing, scheduling, retries small, Redis already present

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "The queue retries failed jobs, so the pipeline is fault-tolerant"
    ✅ Redelivery re-executes the same input; for a deterministic fault that's a crash loop across your whole worker count.
  • 🪞 "Workers dying in rotation means bad hosts or a bad deploy"
    ✅ Correlate by message ID: in the cv-parser the fleet was fine and one resume was the pathogen.
  • ⚠️ Don't ack early to avoid duplicates.
    ↳ Why: deleting before the work turns a crash into permanent data loss; Celery's default early ack is this trade, so use acks_late=True.
  • ⚠️ Don't use redelivery as your transient-retry mechanism.
    ↳ Why: it burns receive counts on network blips and sends healthy jobs to the DLQ.
  • ⚠️ Don't set a huge static visibility timeout.
    ↳ Why: a crashed worker's message stays invisible for hours; heartbeat-extend the outliers instead.
  • ⚠️ Don't ship a DLQ without an alarm and an owner.
    ↳ Why: the crash loop becomes data silently never processed.
  • 🔖 Version: SQS visibility timeout is 0 s–12 h (default 30 s), with a 12 h in-flight ceiling extension can't reset; Celery 5.x for acks_late and task_reject_on_worker_lost.
    ↳ Note: redelivery verified with moto 5.2.3 and boto3 1.43.

🕸️ Connections

Path: idempotency ─▶ queues & workers ─▶ observability

  • Builds on idempotency: at-least-once delivery makes idempotent handlers non-optional.
  • Builds on diagnosing memory: why the cv-parser worker died, and how it was found.
  • Contrasts with reliability mechanics: in-job retries for transient faults; redelivery for crashes.
  • Used by observability: receive counts and DLQ depth as first-class metrics.
  • Same idea elsewhere: RabbitMQ's dead-letter exchanges and Kafka's retry and DLQ topics apply the same cap-and-park defense.

notes.title: Structured Logging & Context Propagation (Structured Logs · contextvars · What Not To Log)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Logging HOWTO · 📘 contextvars · 📘 structlog

⚡ TL;DR

Emit each record as JSON fields, so the aggregator queries user_id=42 instead of regexing text. Carry trace_id in a ContextVar: asyncio gives each task its own copy, while threading.local is shared by every request on the loop.

🧭 Flow: middleware sets trace_id_var for the request ─▶ log.info("event", **fields) ─▶ level gate: filtered records never render ─▶ processors merge context vars and redact PII ─▶ JSON renderer, last ─▶ one line to stdout ─▶ shipper ─▶ aggregator

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Structured vs traditional logging? Machine-parseable key-value records instead of free text: indexable, queryable, correlatable by field.
What's wrong with log.info(f"user {uid} did {x}")? It formats even when filtered out, and it buries queryable fields in an opaque string.
How does trace_id survive await? A ContextVar, copied per task by asyncio; threading.local is shared by every coroutine on the loop.

💡 The idea

Text logs push parsing onto the log platform, with regex pipelines that break the day someone edits a format string; structured records ship fields the aggregator indexes directly. The compounding win is correlation: one trace_id reconstructs a request across the API, workers and the LLM gateway. The trap is where that ID lives. On CPython 3.12, three concurrent requests each stored their ID, awaited, then read it back:

request   threading.local   ContextVar
req-0     req-2             req-0
req-1     req-2             req-1
req-2     req-2             req-2

Every coroutine shares the loop's one thread, so thread-local "per-request" state is really per-worker state, and the last writer wins. The bug never shows in dev, only under concurrency, where it stamps one user's ID on another's logs. ContextVar (3.7+) exists for exactly this: asyncio copies the current context when it schedules each task (the event loop).

The trade: one keyword argument per field and a processor chain buy logs you can query and correlate, and in exchange they become a durable, searchable store you must keep secrets out of.

⚙️ How it works

It's the same stdlib pipeline (logger, filter, handler, formatter) with only the last step changed and fields bound from context instead of interpolated. With plain logging, a custom Filter sets record.trace_id = trace_id_var.get(); structlog does it with the merge_contextvars processor.

💻 Code

import logging, structlog
from contextvars import ContextVar

trace_id_var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("trace_id", default="-")

def add_trace_id(_, __, event_dict):
    event_dict["trace_id"] = trace_id_var.get()     # async-safe: the task's own copy
    return event_dict

structlog.configure(
    processors=[
        structlog.contextvars.merge_contextvars,     # bound context first
        add_trace_id,
        structlog.processors.add_log_level,
        structlog.processors.TimeStamper(fmt="iso", utc=True),
        structlog.processors.format_exc_info,
        structlog.processors.JSONRenderer(),         # ALWAYS last: earlier steps edit the dict
    ],
    wrapper_class=structlog.make_filtering_bound_logger(logging.INFO),
)
log = structlog.get_logger()
# in middleware: trace_id_var.set(request_id)
log.info("llm_request_completed", user_id="u_42", tokens_used=842, latency_ms=1240)

With structlog 26.1.0 that line rendered as {"user_id": "u_42", "tokens_used": 842, "event": "llm_request_completed", "trace_id": "abc-123", "level": "info"}, and a log.debug(...) below the INFO gate produced nothing at all.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Structured logging emits each record as JSON fields, so the aggregator queries by field instead of regexing text. In Python it's the same logging pipeline with a JSON formatter, usually via structlog. The senior point is correlation: a trace_id set in middleware in a ContextVar follows the request across every await, which threading.local can't do because every coroutine shares one thread. Plus a redaction step before the renderer.

Q · Mechanism — How do you propagate request context like trace_id across async boundaries? With contextvars.ContextVar. All coroutines on a worker share one OS thread, so threading.local gives per-worker state, and concurrent requests overwrite each other (all three read req-2 in the test). asyncio copies the current Context whenever it schedules a task, so each task sees the values set in its own flow, including inside gather and create_task. Wire it once: a middleware sets the var, and a structlog processor or a logging Filter copies it into every record. Never a module global, never threading.local, for per-request state.

⚖️ Compare

stdlib logging + JSON formatter structlog
Context binding manual: extra=, a custom Filter first-class: bind(), merge_contextvars
Pipeline logger → filter → handler → formatter an ordered processor chain, JSON renderer last
Dev ergonomics the same JSON everywhere ConsoleRenderer in dev, JSON in prod
Best for minimal dependencies, existing config async services with per-request context

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Structured logging is print(json.dumps(...))"
    ✅ That throws away the pipeline: levels, filters, handlers, per-module tuning, exception formatting.
  • 🪞 "Pre-formatting with f-strings is harmless"
    ✅ It pays even when filtered, and destroys the fields; pass kwargs and let the renderer format survivors.
  • 🔀 Not the same: threading.local vs ContextVar
    ↳ Difference: thread-local is per thread, which in async means per worker; a context variable is per task.
  • ⚠️ Don't log per token on streaming hot paths.
    ↳ Why: 50 tokens/s × 1,000 streams is 50K records/s through a locked pipeline; log stream start and end, and use QueueHandler for extreme rates.
  • ⚠️ Don't log PII without a redaction processor before the renderer.
    ↳ Why: structured logs make user_email indexed and searchable forever.
  • ⚠️ Don't attach full tracebacks reflexively on hot paths.
    ↳ Why: a retained exc_info pins its frames' locals (phantom growth).
  • 🔖 Version: contextvars 3.7+; structlog's stdlib-interop recipe shifts across majors.
    ↳ Note: checked with structlog 26.1.0 on CPython 3.12.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: logging ─▶ structured logging ─▶ observability

  • Builds on logging: the pipeline this note makes production-grade.
  • Builds on the event loop: one thread for all requests is why threading.local fails.
  • Used by observability: OpenTelemetry trace and span IDs ride the same context.
  • Used by ASGI middleware: where the trace ID is set per request.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's MDC with virtual threads and Go's context.Context carry request-scoped values the same way.

notes.title: Observability Instrumentation (OpenTelemetry Spans · Traces · Metrics)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 OpenTelemetry Python: instrumentation · 📘 Semantic conventions for GenAI spans

⚡ TL;DR

LLM instrumentation is span design: a trace per request, a child span per stage, attributes for metadata, events for instants. Record metadata, not content; and record exceptions on the span even when the code swallows them.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Span vs attribute vs event? Span: a duration with a parent. Attribute: a queryable dimension. Event: an instant inside a span.
Where does time-to-first-token go? An event (gen_ai.first_token) on the generate span, not its own span.
How does a swallowed exception stay visible? record_exception(e) + set_status(ERROR) marks it failed though the code returned.

💡 The idea

GenAI semantic conventions name the fields so any OTLP backend reads them; prompts are opt-in behind PII governance. Context crosses await through contextvars, the same mechanism as correlation IDs. With opentelemetry-sdk 1.45.0 and an InMemorySpanExporter, all spans shared the root's trace ID, and the retrieve span whose TimeoutError was caught still ended ERROR with an exception event. GenAI conventions are still in Development: pin the version you emit.

💻 Code

from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.trace import Status, StatusCode

tracer = trace.get_tracer("rag.service")        # exporter wired once, in lifespan

def answer(query: str) -> str:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("rag.query"):                    # the trace root
        with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat gpt-4o-mini") as gen:   # semconv: "{op} {model}"
            gen.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", "gpt-4o-mini")
            gen.add_event("gen_ai.first_token")                         # TTFT: an event
            gen.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", 842)        # metadata, never prompts
        with tracer.start_as_current_span("retrieve") as r:
            try:
                ...
            except TimeoutError as e:                                   # degrade, stay visible
                r.record_exception(e); r.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR))
        return "..."
